realLife: Dropout is a standard regulariser in fully connected layers when data is limited.
summary: Randomly switch off units while training so no unit can lean on another unit's mistakes.
headline: Train with parts missing
overview: At each training step dropout silences a random share of hidden units. The network cannot rely on any one unit being present, which discourages units from co-adapting to quirks of the training set.
At prediction time dropout is switched off. Modern implementations rescale during training so nothing needs changing at test time.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Drop 90% of units at every step. The network is starved: its training loss stays high, and the picture shows it underfitting instead of memorising.

check.question: What does dropout do at prediction time in most libraries?
options: It drops a different half each time

data: Sixty training points from noisy moons and 200 fresh points for testing, through a 2-16-16-1 ReLU network trained 300 passes. The gap between test and train loss is the overfitting signal. Results vary with the random start.
maths: q is the share dropped. Dividing by 1 - q during training keeps the average activation unchanged, so inference uses the full network as is. This is called inverted dropout.

The original paper keeps units with probability p instead and scales weights at test time, so p = 0.5 there means 50% dropped. Combining dropout with batch normalisation can hurt, because dropout shifts activation variance between training and test.
code:
import torch.nn as nn
nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(p=0.5), nn.Linear(16, 1))
model.eval()   # turns dropout off for prediction

sources.title: Li et al.: dropout and batch normalisation disharmony
